clue.text: Wistful writer's riddle broadcast

indicators.note: something broadcast goes out over the air, so we go by how the words are spoken rather than spelt

blocks.note: a pen is a writer, and a riddle is a coarse sieve for soil or grain

explanation.surface: An author's puzzling conundrum, read out on the radio, leaves listeners feeling wistful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riddle' looks like a puzzle, but here it is the gardener's sieve; said aloud, PEN'S SIEVE runs together as PENSIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone wistful is lost in quiet, slightly melancholy thought, which is exactly being thoughtful in that dreamy way.

clue.text: Apparently singular snack for teams

blocks.note: a mid-morning snack is '...', which looks like a plural, so its apparent singular drops the final -ES
football and cricket sides have eleven players each

explanation.walkthrough: Elevenses is the British name for a mid-morning snack; it looks like a plural, so the setter takes its apparent singular. Cricket and football teams are called elevens.
explanation.definitionFit: Sports sides of eleven players are commonly called elevens, and the snack word looks like that word's plural form.

clue.text: Facade's terribly posh for New Town, initially

definitions.note: read as 'Facade is', the possessive-looking 's joining definition to wordplay

indicators.note: something done terribly is done badly, so the letters come out in a wrong, jumbled order
initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the first letters of New and Town

explanation.surface: A smart building facade is dismissed as ghastly and snobbish by someone from a planned New Town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Facade's' reads as 'Facade is', so the 's is a link rather than a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: The facade of a shop is its street-facing front, the glazed display face customers see.

clue.text: Trip finding Venice on yacht, principally, taking a time

indicators.note: principally means first and foremost, so each word supplies only its leading letter

blocks.note: the first letters of Venice, on and yacht
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A holiday sailing boat reaches Venice and takes its time cruising the lagoon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking' simply adds the next piece on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A voyage is a long journey, especially by sea, so it is a kind of trip.

clue.text: Leaves in hot water here?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone abandoned in trouble
setter's reading: the place where tea leaves sit steeping in boiling water

explanation.walkthrough: 'In hot water' suggests disgrace, and 'leaves' a verb of departure; really the leaves are tea leaves brewing.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea leaves are brewed by steeping them in boiling water inside a pot made for the purpose.

clue.text: Levi suffered somewhat, on reflection, gushing

indicators.note: somewhat means only part of something, so the answer is a stretch of letters inside the words
a reflection shows things the wrong way round, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: read right to left, these words contain the answer

explanation.surface: A man called Levi, thinking back on his hardships, becomes emotional and tearful.
explanation.definitionFit: Effusive describes expressing feelings in an unrestrained, overflowing way, just as gushing praise does.

clue.text: Jacket potato and red kale are their starters

indicators.note: starters are what comes first, so each word contributes only its opening letter

blocks.note: the first letters of potato, and, red, kale and are

explanation.surface: A menu: jacket potato with red kale served first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jacket potato' looks like one dish, but 'Jacket' alone is the definition. 'Starters' is a menu word that here means first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A parka is a hooded, padded windproof coat, a type of outdoor jacket.

clue.text: Dash over to meet a German to swap car?

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the word is read back to front

blocks.note: to dart is to dash
ein is German for a

explanation.surface: Hurrying across to meet a man from Germany to exchange vehicles.
explanation.definitionFit: A trade-in is an old vehicle handed over as part payment for a new one, a swap at the dealer; the question mark marks the example.

clue.text: Jargon from flyer heard on the Big Breakfast?

indicators.note: heard means we go by the word as it sounds when spoken, not its spelling

blocks.note: a pigeon is a bird, a flyer
a full English is a large British cooked breakfast of eggs, bacon, sausages and so on

explanation.surface: Odd talk from a bird appearing on The Big Breakfast, a 1990s British morning TV show.
explanation.walkthrough: The Big Breakfast was a Channel 4 morning programme, but here it is the full English fry-up.
explanation.definitionFit: Pidgin English is a simplified mixed language for trade, and jargon is an old term for exactly such hybrid speech.

clue.text: Medicinal plant back at rear of nursery

indicators.note: the rear is the back end, so only the closing letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: to back a horse is to bet on it
on and at both mean located by, as in 'on the coast'
the last letter of nursery

explanation.surface: A herbal remedy grows at the far end of a plant nursery.
explanation.definitionFit: Betony is a purple-flowered herb of the mint family, long used in folk medicine as a remedy.

clue.text: Relaxed popular class by a lake

blocks.note: something in is in fashion
a form is a school class in Britain
taken as written
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A well-liked school group enjoys an easygoing lesson beside a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: In British schools a form is a year group or class.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal means casual and free of ceremony, the same easy manner as relaxed.

clue.text: Joiner is topping worker

indicators.note: topping means cutting off the top, so the first letter of the word is removed

blocks.note: a hand is a labourer, as in farmhand

explanation.surface: A carpenter is a worker who trims the tops of things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joiner' looks like a carpenter but is the grammatical sense: a conjunction joins words.
explanation.definitionFit: The conjunction links words and clauses together, so grammatically it is a joining word.

clue.text: It comes in banks in the main

definitions.text: It comes in banks in the main

blocks.note: surface reading: something deposited in high-street banks, such as money
setter's reading: 'the main' is the open ocean, where thick banks of mist roll in

explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' suggests finance and 'in the main' means mostly; really they are fog banks out on the main, an old word for the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Mist forming over the ocean drifts in dense banks, and the main is a poetic name for the sea.

clue.text: Flimsy material made of some rags

indicators.note: made means fashioned or put together, so the letters are reworked into something new

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cheap, thin fabric stitched together from old scraps of cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Gossamer is a very light, delicate gauzy fabric, or the fine threads of a spider's web.

clue.text: Even innards of basset-hound for the Villa!

definitions.note: a first word of a name, supplied to complete it

indicators.note: even means the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on, taken from inside the word

blocks.note: the even-numbered letters of basset-hound

explanation.surface: Even a dog's guts are fair game for Aston Villa's fans.
explanation.walkthrough: Aston Villa is a Birmingham football club, nicknamed the Villa.
explanation.definitionFit: The club's full name puts this Birmingham district before Villa, so it completes the familiar nickname.

clue.text: Having just one connection travelling via tunnel

indicators.note: things travelling are on the move, so the letters move into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rail traveller going through the tunnel has only a single change of train.
explanation.definitionFit: In chemistry a univalent atom has a valency of one, forming a single bond with other atoms.

clue.text: Whisky from wild archipelago without church

indicators.note: without means lacking, so those letters are taken away
something wild is unruly and out of order, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A single malt distilled in remote, untamed Scottish islands with no kirk in sight.
explanation.walkthrough: Take C and E out of archipelago, then rearrange what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Laphroaig is a peaty single malt Scotch made on Islay, one of the Hebridean islands.

clue.text: A capital girl – by Jove – ripping!

indicators.note: ripping tears something apart, so the letters are pulled into a new order

blocks.note: a girl's name
the Roman god's name, taken as written

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned exclamation that a girl is first-rate: capital, by Jove, ripping!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital', 'by Jove' and 'ripping' all read as dated British exclamations of delight, but 'capital' is the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Sarajevo is the capital city of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

clue.text: Controlling influence of coach during time-off

indicators.note: during means in the middle of a period, so one word sits inside the other

blocks.note: rest is time off work
to coach is to train

explanation.surface: A sports coach keeps a firm hand on players even on their days off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' looks like the definition, a controlling influence on a team; it is the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Restraint is a check or limiting force on behaviour, something that controls actions.

clue.text: Touchy leading economist with reason

definitions.note: emotive means arousing feeling, so 'touchy' in the sense of a sensitive subject

indicators.note: leading means coming first, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the first letter of economist
a motive is a reason for acting

explanation.surface: A prickly top economist insists on a reasoned argument.
explanation.definitionFit: An emotive subject stirs strong feeling, much as a touchy topic is one that easily provokes people.

clue.text: Superior meal, seconds not required

indicators.note: something not required is left out, so that letter is dropped from the word

blocks.note: supper is an evening meal
s is the abbreviation for seconds

explanation.surface: A fine dinner so filling that nobody needs second helpings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seconds' suggests extra helpings, but it is the unit abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Upper means higher in rank or position, as in the upper classes, so it means superior.

clue.text: Graceful and neat, oddly concealing limb

indicators.note: oddly means strangely, so the letters are set out in an unusual order
concealing means hiding something inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
a leg is a limb

explanation.surface: A dancer moving with poise and tidiness, strangely keeping one leg hidden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' tempts a solver to take odd letters; here it rearranges the whole word.
explanation.definitionFit: Elegant means stylish and refined in movement or appearance, which is what graceful conveys.

clue.text: Opposed to a bit from Keats, say

blocks.note: taken as written
a verse is a stanza, a section of a poem by Keats or any poet

explanation.surface: Someone objecting to a passage of Romantic poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks Keats as just one example of a poet.
explanation.definitionFit: To be averse to something is to dislike or be against it, the same as opposed to it.

clue.text: No farewell to learners. In no way

blocks.note: taken as written
ta-ta is a British informal goodbye
L is a learner, from the L-plates on British learner drivers' cars, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A driving instructor refuses to say goodbye to their pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' just attaches the pieces together.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an emphatic negative meaning to no degree whatsoever, the same as in no way.

clue.text: Arab picked up the vernacular

blocks.note: AR is a standard abbreviation for Arab or Arabic
to pick something up is to get it

explanation.surface: An Arabic speaker quickly learnt the local dialect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' hints at a sound-alike, but here it simply means got.
explanation.definitionFit: Argot is the slang or jargon of a particular group, a kind of everyday local speech.

clue.text: Differs showing V-sign

blocks.note: taken as written
Aries is a sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: Someone shows disagreement by making a rude two-fingered gesture.
explanation.walkthrough: A V-sign is a rude British hand gesture, but here V is a letter and the sign is astrological.
explanation.definitionFit: To vary is to be different or change, so something that varies differs.

clue.text: Furniture company no longer has active president

indicators.note: no longer having something means it has been lost, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: the Swedish flat-pack furniture retailer
a is the grammatical abbreviation for active

explanation.surface: A furniture firm has lost its energetic chief executive.
explanation.definitionFit: Ike was the popular nickname of Dwight D. Eisenhower, the thirty-fourth US president.

clue.text: Tops and just one t-shirt for starters

indicators.note: starters come first, so each word gives only its opening letter

blocks.note: single means only one
the first letters of t and shirt

explanation.surface: Shopping for tops, starting with a single tee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tops' looks like a verb or 'the best', but it is clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Singlets are sleeveless vests worn on the upper body, so they are tops in the clothing sense.

clue.text: Unsure a gangster is holding president

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the answer sits whole within the following words

blocks.note: letters running across the three words

explanation.surface: A hesitant mobster has taken a head of state hostage.
explanation.definitionFit: Ronald Reagan was the fortieth president of the United States, serving through the 1980s.

clue.text: Ruin half of Rhodes and Ilium

indicators.note: half means only part, here the back portion of the word

blocks.note: the last three of the six letters of Rhodes
Ilium is the Latin name for ancient Troy

explanation.surface: Ruins on Rhodes and at ancient Troy, two sites of classical Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruin' looks like a noun among ancient sites, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To destroy something is to wreck it completely, the same as to ruin it.

clue.text: Massive group rowing in outskirts of Wallasey

indicators.note: outskirts are the edges of a town, so only the first and last letters are kept
in means inside, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: the first and last letters of Wallasey
an eight is a racing crew of eight rowers

explanation.surface: A big rowing crew training on the water near Wallasey, a town on the Wirral.
explanation.definitionFit: Weighty means heavy, of great weight, which is what massive describes.
